sample.title: The Truth About How Data Centers Use Water And Power To Keep Cool
sample.description:
U.S. voters passed 40 ballot measures putting limits on AI data centers this week, as huge 1GW AI data centers from OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI, Amazon, Google and more push up water and power bills and put a strain on local resources. One of the issues that continues to come up is water usage, which is needed to cool the GPUs inside data centers running AI workloads. Closed-loop liquid cooling keeps water use low inside many modern AI data centers, but external cooling is still needed to move heat outside of the buildings and that requires large amounts of power or water in hot climates. CNBC visited data centers and spoke to researchers to find out the truth about how data centers use water.

sample.title: Krakow shooting leaves six dead, including British citizen | BBC News
sample.description:
An attack in Krakow’s Main Market Square on Saturday has left six people dead. 
 
Police said a 25-year-old man drove into the square "before beginning to fire at random people from his car". 
 
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect is a Polish national.
 
He added that it looks like he held "very radical views" and that everything indicates he was inspired by "far-right ideologies".
 
One of the six people killed in the attack has been identified as a British national.
 
The head of Poland's police force, Marek Boroń, says 16 more people were injured, including two police officers, five foreign nationals and the suspect.
 
Krakow is also holding two days of mourning, with businesses in the city closed today after the attack.

sample.title: Krakow gunman who killed 6 is “ultra-nationalist inspired by far-right ideology” | BBC News
sample.description:
The gunman who has killed six and injured more than a dozen people in Krakow is believed to be an ultra-nationalist inspired by far-right ideology. 

Police said the attacker drove onto Main Market Square, the busy centre of Poland's second largest city, and began randomly firing at people.

The gunman, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, was shot by police, one of whom was critically injured.

The 25-year-old male Polish gunman - described by one minister as "ultra-nationalist" - survived and is in custody.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies were later found at the suspect's home.

The rampage took place in the afternoon in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists. Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out. The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight.
Distressing footage captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect and was then seen falling to the ground.
A Polish minister later said one police officer was fighting for his life and a second was expected to recover from a less serious injury.

The centre of Krakow was locked down as police tended to at least 15 injured people. Some buildings were later evacuated as the attacker's car was searched for explosive devices.

After police identified the gunman and searched his home, the bodies of two women and a man were found.  Donald Tusk said there was "much to suggest" they were the suspect's immediate family members.

Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said of the gunman:  "everything suggests that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultra-nationalist views".

Ben Brown presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Magda Mis in Krakow.
